name: Redefining Success
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Winning by Changing What Winning Means
lesson.summary: A narrower and sneakier cousin of the Moving Goalposts Pattern: retroactively redefining success after a deadline has passed, a trick that only works because Unfalsifiable Timelines leave so much room for after the fact interpretation.
lesson.body:
Moving goalposts describes changing the target before or during the attempt. Redefining success is a narrower and, in some ways, sneakier move: it happens after the fact, once the original outcome is already known, and it works backward from that outcome to a definition that makes it look like a win. If a promised deadline for "breaking modern encryption" passes with encryption fully intact, redefining success is the maneuver where the same period gets described afterward as a success anyway, because a small quantum processor beat a classical computer on some unrelated, artificial benchmark that has nothing to do with encryption.

This tactic depends heavily on the ambiguity discussed in the last chapter. If a prediction had been falsifiable from the start, with a specific criterion nailed down in advance, redefining success afterward would be an obvious and visible cheat, easy for anyone to point out. Because so many big quantum computing predictions are stated in soft, unfalsifiable language, there is room after the fact to select whichever narrower achievement did occur and present it as though it had been the real goal all along. The retroactive substitution is much harder to catch than a goalpost that visibly moves in real time, because there was never a sharp, agreed upon line to notice crossing or not crossing.

A useful real world comparison, familiar outside quantum computing, is a company that promises record breaking growth and then, when growth turns out to be ordinary, announces it has hit a record on some far more specific and previously unmentioned metric, like revenue in a particular subcategory during a particular quarter. Nothing in the announcement is technically false. Everything about it is constructed to obscure that the plain, natural reading of the original promise did not come true. Quantum computing coverage does this with phrases like "quantum advantage" or "quantum supremacy," terms that have accumulated multiple, shifting technical definitions over the years, some far weaker than what a general audience would assume the words mean.

The way to defend against this is to fix the definition of success before the outcome is known, and refuse to accept a definition offered only after the results are in. If a claim was originally about breaking encryption, a later achievement involving an unrelated toy problem does not retroactively validate it, no matter how the announcement is worded. This is exactly the discipline the earlier chapters on the Moving Goalposts Pattern and Unfalsifiable Timelines were building toward: write the prediction down in advance, in falsifiable terms, and hold every later claim of success to that original text rather than to a definition manufactured after the fact.

It is worth being fair here too. Genuine scientific progress often does involve legitimately updating what success looks like as understanding improves, and that is different from redefining success to rescue a failed prediction. The difference is timing and honesty: an update made before the deadline, with the change clearly flagged and the original prediction openly marked as revised, is normal science. A definition that appears only after the deadline has passed, quietly, without acknowledging that anything was originally promised and not delivered, is the pattern this chapter warns about. Keeping the two apart is one of the sharpest tools a skeptical reader can carry into the rest of this guide.
